l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 continues the letter to the Jews in Egypt, recounting records about Jeremiah the prophet, who charged the exiles not to forget the Lord's law amid idols of gold and silver. Jeremiah hid the tabernacle, the ark, and the altar of incense in a cave on the mountain where Moses had gone up, sealed it, and rebuked followers who could not find it, saying the place would stay unknown until God gathers the people and shows mercy. The letter also recalls Moses' and Solomon's sacrifices consumed by fire, Nehemiah's library, and Judas' gathering of scattered books, and invites the recipients to celebrate the purification days. Then the abridger introduces the work: the story of Judas Maccabaeus and his brothers, the temple's purification, and the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and Eupator, drawn from Jason of Cyrene's five books. The abridger explains the aim of condensing them into one book, comparing the labor to a banquet host and a house decorator, and ends by saying a long prologue would be foolish.

l: Jeremiah, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Jeremiah the prophet, according to the records, charged the exiles not to forget the Lord's statutes or be led astray by images of gold and silver. Warned by God, he took the tabernacle, the ark, and the altar of incense into a cave on the mountain where Moses had gone up and sealed the entrance. When followers failed to find the way, he rebuked them, saying the place would remain unknown until God gathers the people and shows mercy.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: God warned Jeremiah to take the tabernacle and ark to the mountain, and is said to be the one who will disclose the hidden things when he gathers his people and shows mercy. He is described as having saved all his people, restored the heritage, kingdom, priesthood, and consecration, and delivered them from great evils and purified the place. The writers hope he will soon have mercy and gather them from everywhere into his holy place.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Judas, along with his brothers, is named as the subject of the history to be abridged, including the purification of the temple and dedication of the altar. Separately, Judas is said to have gathered the books scattered by the war, which remain with the writers.

l: Jason of Cyrene, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Jason of Cyrene is identified as the author who declared the history of Judas Maccabaeus and his brothers in five books. The abridger takes his work as the source to be condensed into one book.

l: abridger (author of the abridgement), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: The abridger says he will condense Jason's five books into one, to attract readers, help those who wish to recall the story, and benefit all. He describes the work as sweat and sleeplessness, compares himself to a banquet host and a house decorator, and leaves exact detail to the original historian. He closes by saying a long prologue before an abridgement would be foolish and begins the narration.

l: cave (Jeremiah's cave), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Jeremiah found a cave and placed the tabernacle, ark, and altar of incense inside, then sealed the entrance. Followers who later tried to mark the way could not find it, and Jeremiah said the place would stay unknown until God gathers the people again.

l: sanctuary in Jerusalem (temple), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Solomon is said to have offered a sacrifice of dedication at the finishing of the temple, and fire came down to consume the burnt offerings. Later the temple, renowned all over the world, is described as recovered and purified through the efforts of Judas and his brothers.

l: books (collected by Nehemiah and Judas), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: Nehemiah, founding a library, gathered the books about the kings and prophets, the writings of David, and letters of kings about sacred gifts. Judas likewise gathered the books scattered by the war, and they are still with the writers, who invite the recipients to send for them if needed.

l: purification of the temple, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: The writers say they are about to celebrate the purification and urge the recipients to celebrate the days. God is said to have purified the place, and the purification of the greatest temple is named among the subjects of the history to be abridged.

l: wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and Eupator, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: The wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator are listed among the subjects of the history. Heavenly manifestations aided the few who fought bravely for Judaism, letting them seize the country, chase the barbarous multitudes, free the city, and restore the laws.

l: Jason of Cyrene's five books, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 2
s: These five books contain the narrative of Judas Maccabaeus, the temple's purification, and the wars. The abridger notes their confusing mass of numbers and abundance of matter, and plans to condense them into one more readable book.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: In Jerusalem, peace and the godly high priest Onias kept the laws, and King Seleucus even paid the sacrificial costs. Simon, guardian of the temple, quarreled with Onias over the city market and, failing to prevail, told Apollonius of Tarsus that the temple treasury held vast sums the king could seize. The king sent his chancellor Heliodorus, who learned from Onias that the treasury held deposits of widows, orphans, and Hyrcanus son of Tobias, totaling four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold, but insisted on confiscating them. As the city prayed in distress, a horse with a golden-armored rider and two radiant young men appeared and scourged Heliodorus to the ground; Onias then offered a sacrifice, the young men told Heliodorus he was spared for Onias's sake, and Heliodorus returned to the king testifying to God's power in that place.

l: Onias, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Onias, the high priest whose godliness and hatred of wickedness kept Jerusalem's laws well observed, disagreed with Simon over the city market. He told Heliodorus that the treasury held deposits of widows, orphans, and Hyrcanus son of Tobias, and that these could not be wronged. Fearing the king might suspect treachery, he offered a sacrifice for Heliodorus's recovery, and the two young men said Heliodorus was granted life for Onias's sake.

l: Heliodorus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Heliodorus, the king's chancellor, was sent to remove the reported money from the Jerusalem treasury and, despite Onias's explanation, declared it must be confiscated. He was struck down by a horse and two scourging young men, left speechless and helpless, then spared after Onias's sacrifice. He offered a sacrifice and vowed vows to God, returned to the king, testified to God's works, and told the king that anyone sent against that place would be scourged because of God's power there.

l: Simon, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin and guardian of the temple, disagreed with Onias about the ruling of the market in the city. Unable to overcome Onias, he went to Apollonius of Tarsus and reported that the treasury held untold sums that could fall under the king's power. Onias called him impious and said his claims were false.

l: Seleucus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: King Seleucus of Asia is said to have borne all the costs of the sacrificial services from his own revenues. After Apollonius informed him of the treasury's money, he appointed Heliodorus to remove it. Later he asked Heliodorus whom he should send to Jerusalem once more, and received a warning about God's power there.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: God, called the Almighty Lord and Sovereign of spirits and of all authority, was invoked by the priests and people as guardian of deposits. He caused a great manifestation that felled Heliodorus and his guards, and he acted marvelously for his own place. Heliodorus afterward testified that God dwells in heaven, watches that place, helps it, and strikes those who come to hurt it.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Jerusalem, the holy city, was inhabited in unbroken peace with its laws well kept. When Heliodorus came to inspect the treasury, the whole city was in distress, with priests, women in sackcloth, and virgins crowding the streets, gates, walls, and windows in prayer. Its fear turned to joy after the divine intervention.

l: sanctuary in Jerusalem (temple), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: The temple was honored by kings with noble presents, and Seleucus paid the costs of its sacrifices. Its sanctity was cited by Onias as reason the trust placed in it could not be violated. After the appearance that struck down Heliodorus, it passed from terror and alarm to joy and gladness.

l: temple (Jerusalem temple), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: The treasury was reported by Simon to be full of untold sums not belonging to the sacrificial accounts. Onias stated it held four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold in deposits. Heliodorus entered with guards to inspect it but was struck down near it before the money was taken.

l: deposits (temple treasury), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Onias explained that the treasury contained deposits of widows and orphans and some money belonging to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man in very high place, totaling four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold. The priests and people prayed that God, who gave the law concerning deposits, would keep them safe for those who deposited them. The text ends with the treasury kept, not confiscated.

l: horse and rider (apparition), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: A horse with a frightening rider, adorned with beautiful trappings, appeared to Heliodorus and his guards near the treasury. The horse rushed fiercely and struck Heliodorus with its forefeet, and the rider seemed to wear complete golden armor.

l: two young men (apparition), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Two young men, notable in strength, beautiful in glory, and splendid in apparel, stood on either side of Heliodorus and scourged him unceasingly with many stripes. They appeared again in the same garments, told him to thank Onias because the Lord granted him life for Onias's sake, and commanded him to proclaim God's sovereign majesty to all. Then they vanished.

l: Heliodorus's scourging and the divine manifestation, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 3
s: Near the treasury, the Sovereign of spirits caused a manifestation that made Heliodorus's guards faint in terror, while Heliodorus fell to the ground in darkness and was carried out on a stretcher, speechless and hopeless. The event made him recognize God's sovereignty and led to joy in the temple. After Onias's sacrifice he was granted life, and he testified to what he had seen.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 recounts how Simon slandered the high priest Onias, who appealed to the king for peace. After Seleucus died and Antiochus Epiphanes became king, Onias's brother Jason bought the high priesthood with promised silver, built a gymnasium under the citadel, and pushed Jerusalem toward Greek customs, so that the priests neglected the altar. Menelaus, Simon's brother, then outbid Jason by three hundred talents, drove him into the country of the Ammonites, and stole temple vessels. When Onias reproved him, Menelaus induced Andronicus to kill Onias by treachery, and Antiochus, grieved, had Andronicus executed. Menelaus's brother Lysimachus committed sacrileges and was killed by the crowd, and Menelaus bribed Ptolemy the son of Dorymenes to win the king over, so that the three men who pleaded against him were sentenced to death while Menelaus kept his office.

l: Simon, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Simon, who had earlier given information about the money against his country, slandered Onias as the one who had incited Heliodorus and caused the evils. His hatred grew until murders were committed through one of his approved agents, and Apollonius the governor was increasing his malice. His brother is Menelaus.

l: Onias, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Onias, the high priest, appealed to the king not to accuse his fellow citizens but to secure the good of all the people, since Simon would not cease his madness. He was supplanted by his brother Jason, later withdrew to a sanctuary at Daphne and reproved Menelaus for the theft of temple vessels, and was lured out by Andronicus under oath and killed. He is described as the benefactor of the city, guardian of his countrymen, and zealot for the laws.

l: Antiochus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Antiochus succeeded Seleucus as king, assented to Jason's offer, visited Jerusalem where Jason received him with torches and shouting, and later accepted Menelaus's higher bid for the high priesthood. He wept over Onias's death and had Andronicus stripped and executed at the place of the crime. He nevertheless was persuaded by Ptolemy son of Dorymenes to acquit Menelaus and sentence the three accusers to death.

l: Jason, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Jason, Onias's brother, supplanted him by promising the king three hundred sixty talents of silver plus eighty more, and offered a further one hundred fifty for a gymnasium and Antiochian citizenship for Jerusalem's inhabitants. He moved his people to the Greek way of life, sent money to the sacrifice of Hercules at Tyre that the bearers diverted to triremes, and received the king magnificently. After Menelaus outbid him he was supplanted and driven as a fugitive into the country of the Ammonites.

l: Menelaus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Menelaus, Simon's brother, was sent by Jason with money to the king, and instead secured the high priesthood by outbidding Jason by three hundred talents of silver. He returned with the passion of a cruel tyrant, did not pay the promised money, stole temple vessels, and had Andronicus kill Onias after Onias reproved him. Accused after the death of Lysimachus, he bribed Ptolemy son of Dorymenes, was acquitted, and remained in office, growing in wickedness.

l: Lysimachus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Lysimachus, brother of Menelaus, was left as deputy in the high priesthood and committed many sacrileges with Menelaus's consent, including the theft of many gold vessels. When the people rose against him, he armed about three thousand men under Hauran, but the crowd with stones, logs and ashes wounded and killed many of them and killed Lysimachus beside the treasury.

l: Andronicus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Andronicus, a man of high rank, was left as deputy by the king when he went to settle the revolt of Tarsus and Mallus. Menelaus gave him stolen gold vessels and asked him to kill Onias, and he gave Onias his right hand with oaths, drew him from the sanctuary, and killed him. The king later stripped him, led him through the city, and put him to death where he had committed the outrage.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Jerusalem's inhabitants were to be registered as citizens of Antioch under Jason's arrangement, and a gymnasium was established under its citadel. The city received Antiochus magnificently with torches and shouting, suffered sacrileges under Lysimachus, and its people rose against him. Its senate sent three men to plead against Menelaus.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: The Jews, along with many of other nations, felt indignation at the unjust murder of Onias, and those in the city appealed to the king against Andronicus, joined by the Greeks. The text says severe calamity overtook those who adopted Greek ways, as the men they imitated became their enemies and punished them. The three men who spoke for the city were condemned, and even some Tyrians provided magnificently for their burial.

l: gymnasium (Jason's gymnasium), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Jason obtained the king's permission to set up a gymnasium and a body of youths trained in it, offering one hundred fifty talents more. He eagerly established it under the citadel itself and had the noblest young men wear the Greek hat. Priests despised the altar and sacrifices and hurried to the wrestling arena after the summons to discus-throwing.

l: Hellenization, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: Jason immediately shifted his own race to the Greek way of life, setting aside royal ordinances favorable to the Jews and introducing new customs forbidden by the law. The text calls it an extreme of hellenization and an advance of foreign religion. Priests despised their fathers' honors and valued Greek prestige, and the text says calamity followed.

l: high priesthood, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: The office was taken from Onias by his brother Jason through a promise of silver, then taken from Jason by Menelaus, who outbid him by three hundred talents. Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus as deputy in it. The text calls Jason an ungodly man and not a high priest, and Menelaus kept the office through the covetous dealings of those in power.

l: murder of Onias, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 4
s: At Menelaus's request, Andronicus used treachery, gave Onias his right hand with oaths, drew him out of the sanctuary at Daphne, and killed him without regard for justice. Jews and many other nations were indignant, and the king wept over Onias's sober and well-ordered life. Andronicus was executed at the very place of the crime, the Lord rendering him the punishment he deserved.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: During Antiochus's second invasion of Egypt, signs of armed cavalry appeared in the sky over the city for almost forty days. On a false rumor of Antiochus's death, Jason attacked Jerusalem with a thousand men and slaughtered his own citizens, forcing Menelaus into the citadel, but he failed to take control and died in exile. Believing Judea in revolt, Antiochus took the city by force, ordered a massacre, and entered the temple with Menelaus as his guide, plundering it. The narrator explains that the Lord's anger over the people's sins permitted this, and that the place shares in the nation's fortunes. Antiochus left governors, including Philip, Andronicus and Menelaus, and sent Apollonius, who killed many on the Sabbath, while Judas Maccabaeus and about nine others withdrew to the mountains.

l: Antiochus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Antiochus made his second invasion of Egypt, then, thinking Judea in revolt, took Jerusalem by force, ordered a massacre, and plundered the temple of eighteen hundred talents with Menelaus as guide. He was arrogant and unaware that the Lord's anger over the people's sins was why he succeeded. He left governors (Philip, Andronicus, Menelaus) and sent Apollonius with an army against the Jews.

l: Jason, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Jason, on a false rumor of Antiochus's death, attacked Jerusalem with a thousand men and slaughtered his own citizens without mercy. He did not win control of the government and fled to the Ammonites. He then ended miserably, imprisoned by Aretas, hated and pursued, and died in exile after seeking shelter among the Lacedaemonians, unmourned and unburied.

l: Menelaus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Menelaus took refuge in the citadel when Jason's assault nearly took the city. He guided Antiochus into the temple, proving himself a traitor to the laws and his country. He was also left as one of the governors and is described as worse than all the rest, exalting himself against his fellow citizens.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Jerusalem was assaulted by Jason, nearly taken, and then captured by force by Antiochus, who had its people slaughtered and enslaved. Philip, a Phrygian, was left as governor there. Apollonius later came to the city, waited for the Sabbath, and killed great multitudes.

l: sanctuary in Jerusalem (temple), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Antiochus entered the temple, called the most holy of all the earth, with Menelaus as guide and took its sacred vessels and offerings, carrying away eighteen hundred talents. The text says the Lord did not choose the nation for the place's sake but the place for the nation's sake. It says the temple shared in the nation's calamities and, at the reconciliation, would be restored with all glory.

l: Apollonius, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Apollonius, called a lord of pollutions, was sent by Antiochus with an army of twenty-two thousand to kill all those of full age and sell the women and boys as slaves. He came to Jerusalem pretending peace, waited for the Sabbath, and had his armed men parade. He put to the sword those who came out to watch and killed great multitudes in the city.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Judas, also called Maccabaeus, withdrew with about nine others to the mountains. They lived like wild animals, feeding on what grew wild so as not to share in the defilement.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: The Jews of Jerusalem suffered Jason's slaughter, then Antiochus's massacre, enslavement and plundering of the temple, and Apollonius's attack on the Sabbath. The narrator attributes their suffering to their sins, which provoked the Lord to a brief anger. Judas Maccabaeus and a small company escaped to the mountains.

l: Jason's assault on Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Prompted by a false rumor that Antiochus was dead, Jason attacked the city with at least a thousand men, routed those on the wall, and nearly took it while Menelaus fled to the citadel. Jason killed his own citizens without mercy. It failed to win him the government, and he fled to the Ammonites in shame.

l: Antiochus's massacre of Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 5
s: Antiochus took the city by force and commanded his soldiers to cut down all in their way and kill those in their houses. In three days eighty thousand were destroyed, forty thousand in close combat, and no fewer were sold into slavery than were slain. Young and old, women, children, virgins and infants were killed.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The king sends an old man of Athens to force the Jews to abandon their ancestral laws and to pollute the sanctuary in Jerusalem, renaming it for Olympian Zeus. The Jews suffer a harsh persecution: they cannot keep the Sabbath or feasts, are forced to eat sacrifices and join Dionysian processions, and those who circumcise their children or keep the Sabbath in caves are killed. The narrator urges readers not to be discouraged, explaining that these calamities are God's chastening of his people rather than their destruction. The chapter then recounts Eleazar, a ninety-year-old scribe, who refuses to eat swine's flesh or even pretend to, and dies under the scourge as an example of nobility and virtue to the young and to the nation.

l: Eleazar, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Eleazar, a principal scribe of advanced age (ninety years), is compelled to eat swine's flesh but spits it out and goes to the instrument of torture willingly. He refuses the offer of his acquaintances to pretend to eat, saying deception would lead the young astray and that he cannot escape God either way. He dies under the blows, saying he suffers in body but gladly in soul out of fear of the Lord, leaving an example of nobleness and virtue.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The Jews are compelled to depart from their fathers' laws, forbidden to keep the Sabbath, observe feasts, or confess themselves Jews, and are forced to eat sacrifices and join the Dionysus procession. Many are killed, including women who circumcised their children and people burned in caves for secretly keeping the Sabbath. The narrator says their suffering is chastening, and that God does not withdraw his mercy or forsake his people.

l: sanctuary in Jerusalem (temple), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The king orders the sanctuary in Jerusalem polluted and named for Olympian Zeus. It is filled with debauchery and reveling by the heathen, who consort with prostitutes and women in the sacred precincts, and the altar is filled with things the laws prohibited.

l: laws of the Jews' fathers (laws of God), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The king's envoy is sent to force the Jews to abandon these laws, and keeping the Sabbath, the ancestral feasts, and circumcision becomes dangerous or deadly. Eleazar upholds them, calling them holy laws of God's ordaining and revered, and dies rather than violate them, setting an example for the young.

l: persecution of the Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: The persecution begins when the king sends an old man of Athens to enforce Greek practices, and a decree extends it to neighboring Greek cities at Ptolemy's suggestion. It includes forced sacrificial eating, forced processions, and killing of those who refuse, such as women who circumcised their children and Sabbath-keepers burned in caves after betrayal to Philip. The narrator interprets it as chastening of the race, not destruction.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: God is presented as the Sovereign Lord who punishes his own people promptly, rather than waiting until their sins reach full measure as with other nations, so that he never withdraws his mercy. Eleazar says no one escapes the hands of the Almighty and that the Lord, who has holy knowledge, sees his suffering and his gladly endured fear of him.

l: swine's flesh, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 6
s: Eleazar is compelled to open his mouth and eat swine's flesh, which is forbidden to him. He spits it out and refuses even the offered pretense of eating, choosing death rather than defilement.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: Seven brothers and their mother are seized at the king's command and tortured to force them to eat swine's flesh. The spokesman brother is mutilated and fried alive, and the next five brothers each die after torture while declaring their hope in resurrection and warning the king of God's judgment. The mother is praised for her courage, exhorting her sons in the language of their fathers and teaching that the Creator will give back their spirit and life. King Antiochus offers the youngest son wealth, honor, and friendship, then urges the mother to persuade him; she instead urges him to accept death, and he defies the king and dies after being treated worse than the others. The mother dies last, and the chapter closes by noting the sacrificial feasts and extreme tortures.

l: Antiochus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: Antiochus, the king, commands the seizure and torture of the seven brothers and their mother, becoming enraged at the spokesman and ordering pans and caldrons heated. He is astonished by the third brother's soul, then tries to win the youngest with oaths of wealth, honor, and friendship and presses the mother to persuade him. When this fails, he handles the youngest worse than the others, and the brothers warn that he will face God's judgment and punishment.

l: seven brothers, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: The seven brothers are taken with their mother and tortured to compel them to eat swine's flesh, but they refuse, saying they are ready to die rather than transgress their ancestors' laws. Each dies in turn, expressing hope in God's compassion, resurrection, and everlasting life, and warning the king of judgment. They also say they suffer for their own sins, and the last hopes their deaths will end God's wrath on the nation.

l: mother (of the seven brothers), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: The mother watches all seven sons die in one day and bears it with courage because of her hope in the Lord, and she is called marvelous and worthy of honorable memory. She exhorts each son in the language of her fathers, saying the Creator who shaped all things will mercifully give back their spirit and life. Urged by the king to persuade the youngest, she instead tells him to accept death so she may receive him again with his brothers; she dies last, after her sons.

l: first brother (spokesman), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: The first brother speaks for the others, declaring they are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of their ancestors. The king has his tongue cut out, scalps him, cuts off his extremities, and fries him alive in a pan while his brothers and mother watch. The family exhorts one another to die nobly, citing Moses' song that God will have compassion on his servants.

l: youngest brother, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: The youngest brother refuses the king's oaths of enrichment, high honor, and friendship if he would abandon his ancestors' ways. Before his mother finishes speaking, he says he obeys the law given through Moses rather than the king, and he tells the king he will not escape God's hands. He gives up body and soul praying that God become gracious to the nation, is handled worse than the rest, and dies pure, trusting the Lord.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: God is called the Lord, the King of the world, the Creator, and the Almighty who sees all things. The brothers and mother trust him to have compassion on his servants, raise those who die for his laws to everlasting life, and punish the king and his descendants. They say his anger against the nation is for rebuke and chastening for their sins, and that he will be reconciled with his servants.

l: laws of the Jews' fathers (laws of God), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: The laws of the ancestors, given to the fathers through Moses, are the reason the brothers refuse to eat swine's flesh and are willing to die. The brothers say they treat their bodies with contempt for the sake of these laws and give up body and soul for them. The youngest says he obeys the law rather than the king's commandment.

l: tortures, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 7
s: The tortures include scourges and cords, heated pans and caldrons, cutting out the tongue, scalping, and removing extremities, and frying the first brother alive. The second brother has the skin of his head pulled off with the hair, and the third has his tongue and hands demanded. The brothers regard the pains as nothing, the king is astonished, and the chapter closes by referring to them as the extreme tortures.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Judas Maccabaeus secretly gathers about six thousand faithful Jews, who pray for the Lord's mercy on the people, sanctuary and city, and he trains them and wins back positions through night raids. Philip alerts Ptolemy, who sends Nicanor and Gorgias with at least twenty thousand troops; Nicanor plans to pay the king's two thousand talent tribute to the Romans by selling Jewish captives. Some Jews flee, but Maccabaeus exhorts the rest to trust almighty God, recalls past divine help, and divides his army among himself and his brothers Simon, Joseph and Jonathan, with Eleazer leading the first band. They defeat Nicanor's army, keep the Sabbath, share spoils with the maimed, widows and orphans, and then defeat Timotheus and Bacchides and burn Callisthenes. Nicanor flees to Antioch and admits that the Jews have One who fights for them.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Judas, also called Maccabaeus, secretly gathers about six thousand faithful Jews, trains them, and carries out night raids that win back important positions. He exhorts his men to trust in almighty God, divides his army into four parts under himself and his brothers Simon, Joseph and Jonathan, and defeats Nicanor. He then shares the spoils with the maimed, widows, orphans and aged.

l: Nicanor, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Nicanor, son of Patroclus, is appointed by Ptolemy to destroy the Jewish race and plans to sell captive Jews at seventy per talent to raise the king's tribute to the Romans. His army is routed, and he removes his glorious apparel and flees like a fugitive slave to Antioch. There he declares that the Jews have One who fights for them and are invulnerable while they follow his laws.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: The Lord is called upon by the Jews to have compassion on the sanctuary, the city and the people, and to remember the blasphemies against his name. His wrath turns into mercy, and the Almighty is said to fight on the Jews' side, humbling Nicanor through those held to be of least account. The Jews bless and thank him for beginning to show mercy to them.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: The Jews are oppressed and threatened with being sold as slaves, and some cowardly ones flee while others sell their goods and pray for those already sold. Those who stay fight under Maccabaeus, win victories, keep the Sabbath and share spoils with the vulnerable. Nicanor finally acknowledges that they are invulnerable because they follow the laws given by their God.

l: Maccabaeus's army, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: About six thousand men are gathered, trained and divided into four parts, three of them led by his brothers with one thousand five hundred men each. They kill more than nine thousand of Nicanor's force, wound and disable most of the rest, and rout them. Afterward they kill more than twenty thousand of Timotheus's and Bacchides's forces, take high strongholds, and store captured weapons in strategic positions.

l: Seleucid army (Nicanor's forces), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Nicanor's army consists of no fewer than twenty thousand men of all nations, joined by the experienced captain Gorgias. More than nine thousand are killed, most of the rest are wounded or disabled, and all are compelled to flee. The army is destroyed.

l: battle with Nicanor, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 8
s: Eleazer reads aloud the sacred book, gives the watchword 'THE HELP OF GOD', and leads the first band to join battle with Nicanor. Because the Almighty fights on their side, the Jews kill more than nine thousand enemies and put the rest to flight. They stop the pursuit because the Sabbath is near, and they take the money of the merchants who had come to buy them as slaves.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Antiochus flees Persia after failing to rob a temple at Persepolis, and on hearing news of Nicanor and Timotheus's forces at Ecbatana he vows to make Jerusalem a graveyard for the Jews. God strikes him with an incurable pain of the bowels, and he falls from his speeding chariot, then suffers worms, falling flesh and a stench that repels his army. Broken in spirit, he acknowledges that mortals must be subject to God and vows to free Jerusalem, make the Jews equal to Athenian citizens, restore and adorn the sanctuary, and become a Jew. When his suffering does not cease, he writes the Jews a letter of supplication appointing his son Antiochus as king and asking for their continued goodwill. He dies in the mountains in a strange land, and Philip, his foster brother, takes the body home and then withdraws to Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt, fearing the son.

l: Antiochus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Antiochus is driven out of Persia after trying to rob a temple at Persepolis, and in his anger vows to make Jerusalem a graveyard of Jews. Struck by God with a bowel affliction and a fall from his chariot, he rots in life, repents with promises to the Jews and the sanctuary, writes them a letter, and dies in a strange land among the mountains.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: God, called the All-seeing Lord, the God of Israel, strikes Antiochus with a fatal and invisible stroke after his boast against Jerusalem. The text presents the king's torment and the stench of his decay as showing that the power was obviously God's, and God no longer shows him pity despite his vows.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: The Jews are the target of Antiochus's threat to make Jerusalem their common graveyard and to leave them unburied for animals and birds. After his affliction he vows to make them equal to citizens of Athens, and he addresses a letter to them as worthy citizens asking for their goodwill toward him and his son.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Jerusalem is the city Antiochus swears to make a common graveyard of Jews when he arrives. In his repentance he vows instead to declare the holy city free, and to adorn the sanctuary and restore its sacred vessels many times multiplied.

l: Antiochus's illness, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: An incurable pain of the bowels with bitter inner torments seizes Antiochus as he finishes his boast, which the text calls just for the torments he had inflicted on others. It worsens after his chariot fall into worms, falling flesh and an intolerable stench, until he is broken in spirit and dies.

l: Antiochus's letter to the Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: Having given up hope for himself, Antiochus writes a letter in the nature of a supplication to the worthy Jewish citizens, wishing them health and prosperity. In it he explains that he has appointed his son Antiochus king, citing his father's precedent, and urges the Jews to keep their goodwill toward him and his son.

l: Antiochus (son of Antiochus), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 9
s: The king's son Antiochus is appointed king in the letter, which says the father often entrusted and commended him to most of the Jews. The father is persuaded that the son will follow his purpose and treat them with moderation and kindness, and Philip fears him after the king's death.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Maccabaeus and his men, led by the Lord, recover the temple and city, tear down foreign altars, build a new altar, and rededicate the sanctuary on the twenty-fifth of Chislev, instituting an annual eight-day festival. Under Antiochus Eupator, who appoints Lysias as governor, Ptolemy Macron kills himself after accusations and Gorgias wages war on the Jews with the Idumaeans' help. Maccabaeus attacks the Idumaean strongholds, kills Simon and his colleagues' fellow officers for taking a bribe, and takes the two towers. When Timotheus invades with a large foreign army, the Jews pray and are aided in battle by heavenly horsemen, killing over twenty thousand. Timotheus flees to Gazara, which the Jews storm on the fifth day, killing Timotheus, Chaereas, and Apollophanes, and they bless the Lord.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Maccabaeus, with the Lord leading, recovered the temple and city and helped cleanse the sanctuary. He attacked the Idumaean strongholds, left a besieging force at two towers, and on learning of the bribery had the traitors killed and took the towers. He prayed before facing Timotheus, was guarded by heavenly horsemen in battle, and besieged Gazara.

l: Maccabaeus's men, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Maccabaeus' men tore down foreign altars, cleansed the sanctuary, and offered sacrifices anew. They fought the Idumaeans and Timotheus, and after four days at Gazara, some young men among them assaulted the wall, burned the towers, and opened the gates to take the city. They then blessed the Lord with hymns.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: The Lord led Maccabaeus and his men in recovering the temple and city. He was implored to spare them from future evils, to fight on their side against the Idumaeans, and to be an enemy to their enemies. He is credited with the victory over Timotheus and blessed for his benefits to Israel.

l: temple (Jerusalem temple), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: The temple and city were recovered by Maccabaeus, and the foreign altars and enclosures were pulled down. The sanctuary was cleansed and a new altar made, with sacrifices, incense, lamps, and show bread restored after two years. Its cleansing fell on the same day, the twenty-fifth of Chislev, that foreigners had profaned it.

l: rededication festival (eight days), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: The Jews observed eight days of gladness in the manner of the feast of tabernacles, recalling how they had recently wandered in mountains and caves like wild animals. They carried leafy wands, branches, and palm fronds and sang thanksgiving hymns. A public statute and decree ordained that the whole nation keep these days every year.

l: Idumaeans, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: The Idumaeans, holding important strongholds, harassed the Jews alongside Gorgias and received refugees from Jerusalem to keep up the war. Maccabaeus's men rushed their strongholds after prayer and killed no fewer than twenty thousand. About nine thousand fled into two strong towers, which were later taken.

l: Simon, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Simon was left by Maccabaeus, with Joseph, Zacchaeus, and their men, to besiege the two towers. Yielding to covetousness, he and his men accepted a bribe and let some of the besieged escape. Maccabaeus accused them of selling their kindred and had them killed as traitors.

l: bribe (seventy thousand drachmas), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Seventy thousand drachmas were paid by some in the Idumaean towers to Simon and his men. In return, some of the besieged were let slip away. Maccabaeus learned of it and executed the men for betraying their kindred.

l: Timotheus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Timotheus, previously defeated by the Jews, gathered large foreign forces and Asian cavalry to take Judea by force. He was routed in battle and fled to the fortress of Gazara, where Chaereas commanded. He was found hidden in a cistern and killed.

l: Timotheus' foreign forces, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Timotheus's army consisted of great multitudes of foreign troops and a considerable Asian cavalry. Driven by passion, they were blinded and thrown into confusion by the heavenly horsemen and cut to pieces. Twenty thousand five hundred were slain, besides six hundred cavalry.

l: five heavenly horsemen, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Five splendid men on horses with golden bridles appeared from heaven to the enemy when the battle grew strong. Two led the Jews and, taking Maccabaeus in their midst, covered him with their armor to guard him from wounds. They shot arrows and thunderbolts at the enemy, blinding and confusing them.

l: Gazara, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: Gazara was a very strong fortress where Timotheus fled and where Chaereas was in command. Those inside trusted its strength and blasphemed during a four-day siege. On the fifth day, young men scaled the wall, burned the towers and blasphemers, opened the gates, and the Jews occupied the city.

l: battle with Timotheus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 10
s: After the Jews prayed in sackcloth and dirt before the altar, they advanced from the city and met Timotheus's army at dawn. The Jews relied on refuge in the Lord, while the enemy was led by passion. Heavenly horsemen intervened, and the enemy was thrown into confusion with over twenty thousand slain.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Lysias, the king's guardian and chancellor, gathers about eighty thousand infantry, all his cavalry, and eighty elephants to attack the Jews, planning to make Jerusalem a Greek home, tax the temple, and sell the high priesthood yearly. He besieges the stronghold of Bethsuron, and Maccabaeus and the people pray for a good angel; a white-clad horseman with golden weapons appears at their head, and the Jews rout the enemy, killing eleven thousand infantry and one thousand six hundred cavalry. Lysias flees, concludes that God fights for the Hebrews, and sues for terms, which Maccabaeus accepts for the common good. The chapter then reproduces letters from Lysias, King Antiochus (to Lysias and to the Jewish senate, mentioning Menelaus), and the Roman ambassadors Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, which grant the Jews their temple, their customs, and amnesty for those who return home.

l: Lysias, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Lysias, the king's guardian, kinsman, and chancellor, marched against the Jews with a huge force intending to Hellenize Jerusalem and profit from the temple and high priesthood, and besieged Bethsuron. After a shameful flight from defeat, he recognized that the Almighty fought for the Hebrews and negotiated terms, promising to persuade the king to befriend them. He then wrote the Jews a letter confirming that he had presented their requests to the king and that what was possible was granted.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Maccabaeus, with the people, prayed for a good angel, then took up weapons first and urged others to risk themselves with him, leading them out willingly. After the victory he accepted Lysias's terms out of care for the common good, and the king allowed whatever requests he submitted in writing.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: The Jews lamented and prayed, followed Maccabaeus to battle, and routed Lysias's army with divine help. They then obtained peace and recognition of their rights through letters from Lysias, the king, and the Roman ambassadors, which restored their temple and their ancestral customs and pledged no molestation for those returning home by the thirtieth of Xanthicus.

l: King Antiochus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: King Antiochus wrote to his brother Lysias, noting that his father wished subjects left undisturbed and that the Jews preferred their own law to Greek customs, and so ordered their temple restored and their ancestral way of life allowed. He also wrote to the Jewish senate granting friendship, permission to use their own foods and laws, and amnesty for things done in ignorance, and said he had sent Menelaus to encourage them.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Jerusalem was the intended target of Lysias's plan to make the city a home for Greeks. Bethsuron, a strong place about five stadia from it, was besieged, and Maccabaeus's men were near Jerusalem when the white-clad horseman appeared.

l: Lysias's army, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Lysias's army numbered about eighty thousand infantry, all his cavalry, and eighty elephants, and he was puffed up by its size. It lost eleven thousand infantry and one thousand six hundred cavalry to the Jews, and the rest fled, mostly wounded and naked.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: God is asked to send a good angel, and is praised as merciful by the Jews when a horseman in white with golden weapons appears. The text says the Lord had mercy on them and fought on their side, and even Lysias concluded that the Almighty fought for the Hebrews, whereas Lysias himself took no account of God's power.

l: Battle at Bethsuron, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: Lysias besieged Bethsuron, a strong place about five stadia from Jerusalem, and Maccabaeus's men advanced against him with the apparition of a white-clad horseman at their head. They fell on the enemy like lions, killing eleven thousand infantry and one thousand six hundred cavalry and putting the rest to flight, Lysias among them.

l: peace terms and royal letters, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 11
s: After the defeat, Lysias agreed to terms recognizing the Jews' rights, and Maccabaeus accepted them. Letters follow from Lysias (dated year 148, Dioscorinthius 24), from King Antiochus to Lysias and to the Jewish senate (year 148, Xanthicus 15), and from the Roman ambassadors Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, who consented to Lysias's grants and asked the Jews to send someone promptly about matters referred to the king.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: After a peace agreement, hostile governors including Timotheus and Nicanor refused to let the Jews live quietly, and the men of Joppa drowned at least two hundred Jews they had invited onto boats. Judas avenged them by burning the harbors and fleets at Joppa and Jamnia, defeated an Arab army and made peace with it, and took the city of Caspin with great slaughter. He then routed Timotheus's huge army, took Carnion, Atergatis's temple and Ephron with heavy killing, and spared Scythopolis because its Jewish residents vouched for its people. After Pentecost he fought Gorgias, whose forces fled, and at Adullam the Jews discovered that fallen comrades had worn idol tokens from Jamnia, which explained their deaths. Judas collected two thousand drachmas and sent it to Jerusalem for a sin offering, an act the text links to belief in the resurrection.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Judas avenges the Joppa murders by burning the harbor and boats there, then does the same at Jamnia, defeats an Arab army and makes peace with it, and takes Caspin, Carnion and Ephron while routing Timotheus's army. He rushes Gorgias's troops with a battle cry and hymns, leads the prayers for the dead at Adullam, and sends two thousand drachmas to Jerusalem for a sin offering, which the text praises as taking thought for the resurrection.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Jews were drowned by the men of Joppa and threatened at Jamnia, but under Judas they win a series of battles. The Jews of Scythopolis testify to their neighbors' kindness, and the army keeps the Sabbath at Adullam and afterwards learns that its fallen carried forbidden idol tokens.

l: Timotheus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Timotheus is one of the governors who would not let the Jews live in peace. He sends his women, children and baggage to Carnion, and his army of 120,000 infantry and 2,500 cavalry flees in terror before Judas. He tricks Dositheus and Sosipater into releasing him by claiming to hold their relatives, and then escapes.

l: men of Joppa, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: The men of Joppa invited the Jews living among them onto boats and drowned no fewer than two hundred of them. Judas burned their harbor and boats at night and killed those who fled there, then withdrew when the gates closed, intending to return and root out the whole community.

l: Jamnites, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: The men of Jamnia intended to do to their Jewish neighbors what Joppa had done. Judas attacked them at night and burned their harbor and fleet, and the glare was seen at Jerusalem, 240 furlongs away.

l: Caspin, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Caspin was a strong city with earthworks and walls and a mixed population. Its people trusted their walls and provisions and blasphemed against Judas's company. Judas called on God, who had brought down Jericho, and took the city with unspeakable slaughter that made the adjoining lake seem filled with blood.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: God is called upon as righteous Judge and Sovereign before Judas's attacks, and the victories at Caspin, Ephron and over the Arabs are credited to his help and will. Judas also calls on him to fight on their side against Gorgias. He is blessed as the one who makes hidden things manifest when the idol tokens are found.

l: Gorgias, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Gorgias, governor of Idumaea, came out with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry after Pentecost. Dositheus of Bacenor's company seized him by the cloak, but a Thracian horseman disabled Dositheus's shoulder and Gorgias escaped to Marisa. Judas then attacked his troops unexpectedly and put them to flight.

l: idol tokens of Jamnia, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Consecrated tokens of the idols of Jamnia were found under the garments of each of the dead Jewish soldiers when they were collected at Adullam. The law forbids Jews to have anything to do with them, and all understood this was why the men had fallen.

l: sin offering for the dead, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Judas took up a collection man by man totaling two thousand drachmas of silver and sent it to Jerusalem to offer a sacrifice for sin. The text says he did this that the dead might be released from their sin, and calls the act holy and godly.

l: resurrection, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: The text says Judas acted well and honorably in taking thought for the resurrection when he sent the offering. It argues that praying for the dead would be superfluous and idle if he did not expect the fallen to rise again.

l: fallen Jewish soldiers, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 12
s: Some Jews fell in the battle against Gorgias. When Judas's men gathered the bodies to bring them to their ancestors' tombs, they found idol tokens from Jamnia under each one's garments. The army prayed that the sin be blotted out, and an offering was sent to Jerusalem on their behalf.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: In the 149th year, Antiochus Eupator marches against Judea with Lysias and an enormous army, joined by the hypocritical Menelaus, whom the king has put to death at Beroea by being pushed into a tower of ashes. Judas leads the people in three days of prayer and fasting, then camps at Modin and leads a night raid on the king's pavilion, killing two thousand men and felling the leading elephant. The king's attack on the fortress at Bethsura fails, and the traitor Rhodocus is caught and imprisoned. Hearing that Philip has become reckless in Antioch, the king makes peace with the Jews, honors the sanctuary, receives Maccabaeus kindly, and leaves Hegemonides as governor. The men of Ptolemais resent the treaty, but Lysias pacifies them and returns to Antioch.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Judas, hearing of the king's advance, commanded the people to call on the Lord day and night, and after three days of prayer consulted the elders and camped at Modin. He gave the watchword "VICTORY IS GOD'S" and led a chosen force of the bravest young men in a night attack on the king's pavilion. He also sent necessary supplies to those inside Bethsura, and was later graciously received by the king as Maccabaeus.

l: Antiochus Eupator, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Antiochus Eupator came against Judea with a huge force and, stirred up against Menelaus, ordered him put to death at Beroea. After the Jewish night raid and a failed attack on Bethsura, he learned Philip had become reckless in Antioch, made peace with the Jews, offered sacrifice, honored the sanctuary, and left Hegemonides as governor. He then went to Ptolemais, where he faced displeasure over the treaty.

l: Lysias, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Lysias, the king's guardian and chancellor, accompanied Antiochus with a great army and informed him that Menelaus was the cause of all the evils. At Ptolemais he defended the treaty, persuaded and pacified the angry people, gained their good will, and departed to Antioch.

l: Menelaus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Menelaus joined the king's expedition and with great hypocrisy encouraged Antiochus, hoping to be set over the government. Lysias blamed him for all the evils, and the king had him taken to Beroea and pushed into a tower of ashes, so that he died without a grave, justly, since he had sinned against the altar whose fire and ashes were holy.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: God is called the King of kings, who stirred up Antiochus's anger against Menelaus, and the merciful Lord and Lord of the world to whom the people prayed with weeping and fasting. Judas committed the decision to him, and the text credits the Lord's protection with the dawn victory that gave Judas help.

l: Bethsura, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Bethsura was a strong Jewish fortress that the king attacked; he advanced, was turned back, failed, and was defeated. Judas sent necessary supplies to those inside, and the king later negotiated with them a second time, giving his hand and taking theirs.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: The Jews, facing the loss of law, country, and temple, fasted and prayed for three days and then fought under Judas, showing exceeding boldness that gave the king a taste of their courage. Rhodocus from their ranks betrayed secrets to the enemy and was arrested and imprisoned. In the end the king swore to acknowledge all their rights and made peace with them.

l: king's army (Antiochus Eupator's army), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: The army numbered one hundred ten thousand infantry, five thousand three hundred cavalry, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred scythed chariots for each of its two commanders. Judas's night raid killed about two thousand men, brought down the leading elephant, and filled the army with terror and alarm. It was later turned back at Bethsura and put to the worse in attacking Judas's forces.

l: night attack on the king's pavilion, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: Judas led a chosen force of the bravest young men against the king's pavilion by night with the watchword "VICTORY IS GOD'S". They killed about two thousand men and brought down the leading elephant along with the man in its tower. The army was filled with terror and the attackers departed with good success at dawn, attributed to the Lord's protection.

l: peace treaty between Antiochus and the Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 13
s: After hearing Philip had become reckless in Antioch, the king made an overture of peace, swore to acknowledge all the Jews' rights, offered sacrifice, and honored the sanctuary and the place. He left Hegemonides as governor from Ptolemais to the Gerrenians. The men of Ptolemais, indignant against the Jews, wanted to annul the articles, but Lysias persuaded and pacified them.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Demetrius, son of Seleucus, takes the country, and the former high priest Alcimus comes to him with gifts and accuses Judas Maccabaeus and the Hasidaeans of sedition. Demetrius sends Nicanor to Judea with orders to kill Judas, scatter his followers, and install Alcimus as high priest. Nicanor, impressed by Judas's men, makes a covenant with him and even befriends him, urging him to marry and settle, until Alcimus reports this to Demetrius, who orders Judas sent to Antioch as a prisoner. Nicanor turns harsh, Judas hides, and Nicanor threatens the priests that he will level the temple and build a temple to Dionysus unless Judas is handed over, while the priests pray for the temple's protection. Nicanor then sends soldiers to seize Razis, an elder called Father of the Jews, who tries to kill himself rather than be taken and dies after a gruesome struggle, calling on the Lord of life and spirit.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Judas is denounced by Alcimus as the leader of the seditious Hasidaeans, and Demetrius orders Nicanor to kill him. After a covenant with Nicanor he is kept in his company and urged to marry and settle, but when Nicanor turns harsh he gathers men and hides. Nicanor then demands that the priests hand him over.

l: Demetrius, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Demetrius sails into the harbor of Tripolis with an army and fleet, takes possession of the country, and has made away with Antiochus and Lysias. Persuaded by Alcimus and his friends, he sends Nicanor to kill Judas and install Alcimus, and later, enraged by Alcimus's accusations, orders Nicanor to send Judas to Antioch as a prisoner.

l: Alcimus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Alcimus, a former high priest who had willfully polluted himself, brings Demetrius a gold crown, a palm and olive boughs and accuses Judas and the Hasidaeans of sedition. He is to be set up as high priest, and he later falsely tells Demetrius that Nicanor is disloyal for naming Judas his successor, using the covenants as evidence. The text calls him a most wicked man.

l: Nicanor, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Nicanor, formerly master of the elephants, is made governor of Judea and sent to kill Judas. He instead makes a covenant with Judas and befriends him, but after Demetrius's rebuke he plots by strategy, then threatens to level the temple and build one to Dionysus. He sends over five hundred soldiers against Razis.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Jews who had driven Judas into exile flock to Nicanor, while the others sprinkle dirt on their heads and pray to God when Nicanor advances. Their priests swear they do not know where Judas is and pray for the temple, and Razis, one of their elders, is hunted down by Nicanor's soldiers.

l: Razis, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Razis is an elder of Jerusalem, well reported and called Father of the Jews, who had earlier risked body and life for the Jewish religion. Nicanor sends over five hundred soldiers to seize him, and he tries to fall on his sword, leaps from the wall, and tears out his bowels, calling on the Lord of life and spirit to restore them before he dies.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: The Jews pray to God as the one who established his people forever and makes his presence manifest. The priests call him Lord of the universe, in need of nothing, who always fights for the nation, and ask him to keep the temple undefiled, and Razis calls on him as Lord of life and spirit.

l: temple (Jerusalem temple), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: Nicanor comes to the great and holy temple during the sacrifices and swears to level it, break down the altar, and build a temple to Dionysus unless Judas is delivered. The priests pray that God keep this recently cleansed house undefiled forever.

l: covenants (between Nicanor and Judas), The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 14
s: After pledges are exchanged and the troops agree, a meeting is held with armed men posted by Judas as a precaution, and the covenants are made. Alcimus takes possession of them and uses them to accuse Nicanor, so Demetrius is displeased and orders Judas sent as a prisoner. Nicanor is troubled at annulling the articles, since Judas had done no wrong.

l: The Second Book of the Maccabees, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Nicanor, learning that Judas and his men are near Samaria, plans to attack on the Sabbath and mocks the Jews who ask him to honor the day, claiming to be a sovereign on earth. Judas Maccabaeus trusts in the Lord, encourages his company with the law, the prophets and a dream in which Onias and Jeremiah appear and Jeremiah gives Judas a gold sword. Before the battle Judas prays, recalling the angel who destroyed Sennacherib's army under Hezekiah, and asks for a good angel to be sent. Judas's men fight with their hands and pray in their hearts, kill at least thirty-five thousand, and find Nicanor dead in armor. Judas has Nicanor's head, hand and arm taken to Jerusalem, displayed, and hung from the citadel, the people decree that the thirteenth of Adar be kept as a day of honor, and the author closes his book with remarks on his style.

l: Nicanor, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Nicanor resolves to attack Judas on the Sabbath, refuses the Jews' plea to honor the day, and declares himself a sovereign on earth who commands them to bear arms. He plans a monument of victory, advances with trumpets and victory songs, and is found dead in full armor after the battle. His head, hand and arm are cut off and taken to Jerusalem, his tongue is cut out, and his head and shoulder are hung from the citadel.

l: Judas Maccabaeus, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Judas trusts unceasingly in the Lord's help, encourages his men with the law, the prophets and a dream of Onias and Jeremiah, and receives a gold sword from Jeremiah in the vision. He prays to the Lord before the battle, citing the angel sent in Hezekiah's time, and after the victory orders Nicanor's head, hand and arm taken to Jerusalem and displayed. He is described as the foremost champion of his fellow citizens, loyal to them since youth.

l: Judas's company, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Judas's company is encouraged by his words and the dream, and resolves to bear down on the enemy and settle the matter hand to hand, fearing most for the sanctuary. They join battle with invocation and prayer, kill no less than thirty-five thousand, and return rejoicing, finding Nicanor dead.

l: Jews, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: Some Jews compelled to follow Nicanor plead with him to honor the Sabbath, saying the living Lord in heaven commanded the seventh day. After the victory the people bless the Lord in their ancestors' language and, in a common decree, ordain that the thirteenth day of Adar be marked with honor, the day before the day of Mordecai. The city is said to have been held by the Hebrews from that time on.

l: God, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: The Lord is named by the Jews as the living Sovereign in heaven who commanded the seventh day to be kept. Judas calls on him as the one who works wonders and gives victory to the worthy, and asks him to send a good angel as he once did against Sennacherib. He is blessed as having manifested himself and kept his own place undefiled.

l: battle between Judas and Nicanor, The Second Book of the Maccabees, Chapter 15
s: The armies join battle with Nicanor's troops set in array, elephants at a convenient post and cavalry on the flanks. Nicanor's side advances with trumpets and songs while Judas's side fights with prayer, killing no less than thirty-five thousand men. The battle ends with Nicanor found dead in full armor.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 addresses the judges of the earth, urging them to love righteousness and to seek the Lord with a good mind and singleness of heart. It says wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil, and that she, as a spirit who loves man, does not leave a blasphemer unpunished because God witnesses his heart and hears his tongue. The spirit of the Lord fills the world and knows what is said, so no unrighteous speech or murmuring stays hidden, and Justice will convict wrongdoers. The audience is warned against slander and against drawing death upon themselves, since God did not make death and created all things to have being. The chapter ends by saying righteousness is immortal, while ungodly men summon death with their hands and words, treat him as a friend, and make a covenant with him.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 1
s: The Lord is to be sought with a good mind and singleness of heart, and he is found by those who do not test him and manifested to those who trust him. His spirit has filled the world, and he is witness of each person's inmost self, overseer of the heart and hearer of the tongue, so no secret utterance or murmuring escapes him. God did not make death, takes no delight when the living perish, and created all things that they might have being.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 1
s: Wisdom is described as a spirit who loves man, but she will not enter a soul that devises evil nor dwell in a body enslaved by sin. She does not hold a blasphemer guiltless for his lips. A holy spirit of discipline is said to flee deceit and thoughts without understanding.

l: judges of the earth, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 1
s: The judges of the earth are directly addressed and commanded to love righteousness, to think of the Lord with a good mind, and to seek him in singleness of heart. They are also warned to beware of unprofitable murmuring and slander, and not to court death or draw destruction on themselves by the works of their hands.

l: the ungodly, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 1
s: Ungodly men are said to be searched out in their counsels, and the sound of their words comes to the Lord to bring their lawless deeds to conviction. By their hands and words they summon death, deem him a friend, pine away, and make a covenant with him, being worthy to belong with him.

l: death, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 1
s: Death was not made by God, and God does not delight when the living perish. Hades has no royal dominion upon earth. Ungodly men summon death with their hands and words, regard him as a friend, and make a covenant with him.

l: righteousness, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 1
s: Righteousness is declared immortal. The judges of the earth are urged to love it, and it stands in contrast with the ungodly, who summon death.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 presents the reasoning of the ungodly, who believe life is short, random, and ends in oblivion with no release from Hades. From this they conclude that they should enjoy wine, perfumes, flowers, and revelry, and should oppress the righteous poor, the widow, and the aged, making their own strength the law. They single out the righteous man, who annoys them by reproaching their sins, claiming knowledge of God, and calling himself God's child, and they plot to test him with insult, torture, and a shameful death to see whether God will deliver him. The narrator declares that they were led astray and blinded by their wickedness, not knowing God's mysteries or the prize for blameless souls. The chapter closes by stating that God created man for incorruption in the image of his own everlastingness, and that death entered the world through the devil's envy and is experienced by those who belong to him.

l: the ungodly (those who speak in verses 1-20), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: The ungodly reason that life is short, chance-born, and ends in ashes and forgetfulness, and so they resolve to revel and to oppress the righteous poor, the widow, and the old. They plot against the righteous man to test whether God will save him, and the narrator says they were led astray and blinded by their wickedness, not knowing God's mysteries or the reward for blameless souls.

l: the righteous man, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: The righteous man is targeted by the ungodly because he reproaches them for sins against the law and their training, lives differently, avoids their ways as uncleanness, calls the end of the righteous happy, and boasts that God is his father. They plan to lie in wait for him, test him with insult and torture, and condemn him to a shameful death to see if God, as his protector, will deliver him.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: God is claimed by the righteous man as his father, and the ungodly mockingly suppose that if the righteous man is his son, God will uphold and deliver him from his adversaries. The narrator states that God created man for incorruption, made him an image of his own everlastingness, and has mysteries and a prize for blameless souls that the ungodly do not know.

l: death, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: The ungodly view death as a final, irreversible end, sealed so that no one turns it back, after which the person is as though never born. The narrator counters that God made man for incorruption and that death entered the world through the devil's envy, and is experienced by those who belong to the devil.

l: enjoyment of pleasures (hedonistic revelry), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 2
s: The ungodly urge one another to enjoy the good things that exist, filling themselves with costly wine and perfumes, crowning themselves with rosebuds, and leaving tokens of mirth everywhere, since this is their portion and lot. This revelry is paired with their resolve to oppress the righteous and is part of the reasoning the narrator calls unsound.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 contrasts the fates of the righteous and the ungodly. The righteous are held in God's hand, appear to the foolish to have died but are at peace, and are tested by God like gold in a furnace, then accepted, made to shine, and given authority over nations. The ungodly, who neglected righteousness and despised wisdom, are punished according to their reasoning, with futile hopes and works, foolish wives, wicked children, and cursed descendants. The chapter says the undefiled barren woman and the faithful eunuch are blessed with fruit and a delightful inheritance in the Lord's sanctuary. Children of adulterers are said not to reach maturity, to be without honor in old age or hope if they die young, and to share in the grievous end of an unrighteous generation.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: God holds the souls of the righteous in his hand, tests them like gold in the furnace, and accepts them as a whole burnt offering, finding them worthy of himself. He is said to reign over them forever, to examine souls and give the barren undefiled woman fruit, and to give the faithful eunuch a precious gift and an inheritance in his sanctuary.

l: the righteous, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: The righteous are in God's hand and untouched by torment; though the foolish think they died, they are in peace and their hope is full of immortality. After bearing a little chastening they receive great good, shine in their visitation, judge nations, rule over peoples, and live with God in love, understanding truth.

l: the ungodly, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: The ungodly neglected righteousness and revolted from the Lord, and they will be punished as their reasoning deserves. Their hope is void, their toils unprofitable and their works useless, and their wives are foolish, their children wicked and their descendants cursed.

l: parents of unlawfully conceived children, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 3
s: Children of adulterers will not come to maturity, and the seed of an unlawful union will vanish away. If they live long they will not be esteemed and their old age will lack honor, and if they die young they will have no hope or consolation on the day of judgment.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 contrasts childlessness joined with virtue against the numerous offspring of the ungodly. Virtue brings immortality, is imitated and longed for, and triumphs forever, while the ungodly's illegitimate offshoots are compared to shaky branches that are broken, bear useless fruit, and testify against their parents. A righteous man who dies early is at rest, because true old age is measured by understanding and an unspotted life, not by years. God, pleased with him, took him away from wickedness so that evil would not corrupt his soul. The peoples fail to understand this, but the ungodly will see the wise man's end, be scorned by the Lord, be dashed to the ground, and be convicted by their own lawless deeds.

l: virtue, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: Virtue is said to make childlessness better than a large family, since its memory brings immortality and is recognized before God and men. People imitate it when present and long for it when gone, and it marches crowned in triumph, victorious in the contest for undefiled prizes.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: God is pleased with the righteous man's soul, loves him, and takes him away from among sinners so that evil cannot corrupt him. He keeps the wise man safe with a purpose the ungodly do not grasp, extends grace and mercy to his chosen, and visits his holy ones. He laughs the ungodly to scorn and dashes them to the ground.

l: the ungodly, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: The ungodly watch the wise man's end without understanding the Lord's plan for him, and they despise what they see. They will become a dishonored carcass and a reproach among the dead, will be shaken from their foundations and left waste, and their memory will perish. Their long years of old age are condemned by the quickly perfected righteous.

l: brood of the ungodly (offspring), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: The multiplying brood of the ungodly is of no profit, and their illegitimate offshoots do not take deep root or gain a sure hold. They are compared to branches that flourish briefly but are shaken and uprooted by wind, broken off before maturity, and bear useless, unripe fruit. Unlawfully conceived children also witness against their parents when investigated.

l: righteous man, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: The righteous man is found well-pleasing to God, loved, and transported from among sinners so that evil would not change his understanding or deceive his soul. Even if he dies before his time, he is at rest, and having been made perfect quickly, he fills a long time. Dead, he condemns the living ungodly.

l: honorable old age, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: Honorable old age is defined not by length of time or number of years. Understanding is the gray hair of men, and an unspotted life is ripe old age.

l: final judgment of the ungodly, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: The ungodly will come with coward fear when their sins are counted, and their lawless deeds will convict them to their face. The Lord will dash them speechless to the ground, shake them from their foundations, leave them utterly waste and in anguish, and their memory will perish.

l: early death of the righteous, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 4
s: The early death of the righteous man is presented as rest rather than loss, since he was caught away lest wickedness corrupt him. Because his soul pleased the Lord, he hurried out of the midst of wickedness. The peoples see it without understanding, but it will condemn the long-lived unrighteous.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 describes the righteous man standing boldly before those who once afflicted him and dismissed his labors. Seeing him, they are terrified and amazed at his salvation, and they lament that they mocked him and went astray from the way of truth, comparing their vanished pride and riches to a shadow, a ship's wake, a bird's flight, and an arrow's path. The ungodly's hope is likened to chaff, foam, and smoke, while the righteous live forever with their reward in the Lord and receive a royal crown and diadem from his hand.
