The Lord takes zeal, righteousness, impartial judgment, holiness, and wrath as armor and weapons, and the whole creation joins him in battle against his enemies with lightning, hailstones, sea, rivers, and a mighty wind, so that lawlessness desolates the land and overturns the thrones of princes.

l: the righteous man, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: He stands in great boldness before those who afflicted him and made his labors of no account. His persecutors are terrified at the sight of him and amazed at his salvation, and they admit they once saw his life as madness and his end as without honor, yet he is counted among the sons of God and has a lot among the saints.

l: those who afflicted the righteous man, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: They see the righteous man, are troubled with terrible fear, and groan in repentance, confessing that they derided him, thought him mad, and went astray from the way of truth. They say their arrogance, riches, and boasting profited nothing, that they traveled the paths of lawlessness and destruction without knowing the Lord's way, and that they were consumed in their wickedness.

l: the righteous, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: The righteous live forever, with their reward in the Lord and the care for them with the Most High. They will receive the crown of royal dignity and the diadem of beauty from the Lord's hand, covered and shielded by his right hand and arm.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: The Lord holds the reward of the righteous, crowns them, and shields them with his right hand and arm. He takes up zeal, righteousness, impartial judgment, holiness, and stern wrath as armor and weapons, and goes out to punish his enemies with the universe fighting alongside him.

l: the ungodly's fleeting prosperity, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: The wicked admit that their arrogance, riches, and boasting all passed away like a shadow, a rumor, a ship's wake, a bird's flight path, or an arrow's trail through air, leaving no trace. The ungodly man's hope is compared to chaff carried by wind, foam vanishing before a tempest, smoke scattered by wind, and the remembrance of a guest who stays one day.

l: divine armor (the Lord's armor), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: The Lord takes his zeal as complete armor, puts on righteousness as a breastplate, wears impartial judgment as a helmet, and takes holiness as an invincible shield. He also sharpens stern wrath as a sword.

l: creation, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: The whole creation is made the Lord's weapons to punish his enemies, and the universe goes with him to fight against his frenzied foes. The sea is angered against the wicked and rivers sternly overwhelm them.

l: storms and elements (weapons against the wicked), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 5
s: Shafts of lightning fly with true aim from the clouds like shots from a well-drawn bow, and wrath-filled hailstones are hurled as from a catapult. The sea's water and rivers overwhelm the wicked, and a mighty wind winnows them away like a tempest, leaving the land desolate.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 6
s: The speaker addresses kings, judges, and rulers, reminding them that their dominion comes from the Lord and the Most High, who will examine their works and plans. Because these officers of his kingdom did not judge rightly, keep the law, or follow God's counsel, a stern and swift judgment will fall on those in high places, while the lowly may be pardoned and the mighty will be mightily tested. The speaker urges the princes to desire his words and learn wisdom, describing Wisdom as radiant, easily found by those who love and seek her, and meeting the worthy on their paths. Desire for instruction is called the beginning of Wisdom, leading through love and observance of her laws to immortality, closeness to God, and a kingdom. The speaker promises to explain what Wisdom is and how she came into being without hiding mysteries, and says a multitude of wise men is salvation to the world and an understanding king is stability for his people.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 6
s: God, called the Lord, the Most High, and the Sovereign Lord of all, is the source of the rulers' dominion and sovereignty. He will search out their works and plans, will not be impressed by anyone or show deference to greatness, and made and cares about both small and great. Immortality brings closeness to him.

l: kings and rulers (the addressees), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 6
s: Kings, judges, rulers, and princes are told that their dominion was given by the Lord and that, as officers of his kingdom, they failed to judge rightly, keep the law, or walk in God's counsel. They face a stern, swift judgment and are urged to desire the speaker's words, learn wisdom, and honor her so that they may reign forever.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 6
s: Wisdom is described as radiant and unfading, easily seen by those who love her and found by those who seek her. She anticipates those who desire her, sits at the gates of those who rise early to seek her, and goes about meeting the worthy graciously. Her beginning is desire for instruction, which is love, which is observance of her laws, leading to immortality and a kingdom; the speaker promises to explain what she is and how she came into being, and says envy has no fellowship with her.

l: judgment, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 6
s: Judgment is said to come awfully and swiftly, and sternly, upon those in high places because the rulers did not judge rightly or keep the law. The lowly may be pardoned in mercy, but the mighty will be mightily tested, and scrutiny of the powerful is strict. Those who kept holy things in holiness and were taught them will find what to say in defense.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 7
s: In Chapter 7 the narrator, a king, declares that he is mortal like everyone else, descended from the first-formed man, formed in his mother's womb, and born with the same cry as all people. He says he prayed and was given understanding and a spirit of wisdom, which he valued above sceptres, thrones, riches, gems, health, beauty and light. He credits God as the guide of wisdom and the giver of unerring knowledge of the universe, including the elements, times and seasons, stars, creatures, winds, plants and roots. Wisdom is described as the architect of all things and as a spirit that is subtle, pure, all-powerful and all-surveying, a breath of God's power, a reflection of everlasting light and an image of his goodness. The chapter ends by saying that God loves the one who dwells with wisdom and that wisdom is fairer than the sun, since night overcomes daylight but evil does not prevail against wisdom.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 7
s: Wisdom came to the narrator when he asked, and he preferred her to thrones, riches, gems, health, beauty and light, since all good things came with her. She is described as the architect of all things, a quick, holy, subtle and pure spirit that pervades everything, a breath of God's power, a reflection of everlasting light and an image of his goodness. Though one, she can do all things and renews them, passes into holy souls to make them friends of God and prophets, and is fairer than the sun, for evil does not prevail against her.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 7
s: God is said to guide even wisdom, to correct the wise, and to hold both people and their words in his hand. He gave the narrator unerring knowledge of the things that are, and he loves nothing so much as one who dwells with wisdom. Wisdom is called a breath of his power, an emanation of his glory, and an image of his goodness.

l: speaker (the king, son of God's handmaid), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 7
s: The narrator, who speaks as a king, says he is mortal like everyone else and shares the same birth and departure as all men. He prayed and was given understanding and a spirit of wisdom, which he chose over sceptres, thrones, riches and light. He learned all things secret and manifest from wisdom, shares her without grudging, and asks God to let him speak God's judgment and think thoughts worthy of what he has received.

l: knowledge of the natural world, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 7
s: The narrator says God gave him unerring knowledge of the structure of the universe and the operation of the elements. This covers the beginning, middle and end of times, solstices and seasons, the circuits of years, the positions of stars, living creatures, wild beasts, winds, the thoughts of men, plants and the virtues of roots. He says he learned all things secret or manifest because wisdom, the architect of all things, taught him.

l: mortality and common human birth, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 7
s: The narrator describes himself as a descendant of the first-formed man, formed as flesh over ten months in his mother's womb, born drawing the common air and uttering the same first cry as everyone. He was nursed in swaddling clothes, and he concludes that no king had a different beginning, since all men share one entrance into life and a common departure.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: Chapter 8 is a first-person speech in which the speaker praises wisdom and describes his love for her, seeking her as a bride. He says wisdom reaches through all things, lives with God and is loved by him, and is richer and more profitable than any possession, teaching soberness, understanding, righteousness, and courage. The speaker lists what he expects from taking her to live with him: counsel in cares, glory and honor among elders and rulers, authority over peoples and nations, and rest at home. He also expects immortality and an eternal memory, and he reasons that immortality is akin to wisdom. Recognizing that he cannot possess wisdom unless God gives her, he pleads with the Lord with his whole heart, and the chapter ends as his prayer begins.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: Wisdom reaches from one end to the other with full strength and orders all things well. She lives with God, is loved by the Sovereign Lord, is initiated into his knowledge, chooses his works, and is described as the maker and architect of things that exist. She teaches soberness, understanding, righteousness, and courage, knows the past and foresees the future, and is sought by the speaker as a bride, counselor, and companion, though he says she must be given by God.

l: the speaker (narrator), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: The speaker says he loved wisdom from his youth, sought her as a bride, and resolved to live with her as a source of counsel and comfort. He anticipates glory, honor among elders, admiration from rulers, rule over peoples, and immortality through her. He describes himself as a clever child with a good soul who came into an undefiled body, and concludes that he can have wisdom only if God gives her, so he pleads with the Lord with his whole heart.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: God is called the Sovereign Lord of all, who loves wisdom, and she lives with him and is initiated into his knowledge. The speaker recognizes that God is the one who must give wisdom and that grace comes from him, and he implores the Lord in prayer at the chapter's end.

l: immortality, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 8
s: The speaker expects to gain immortality because of wisdom, together with an eternal memory left to those who come after him. He reasons that immortality is in kinship to wisdom, which is part of why he seeks to take her to himself.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 9
s: In Chapter 9, a king prays to the God of his ancestors and Lord of mercy, who made all things by his word and formed man by his wisdom to have dominion and rule in holiness and righteousness. The speaker, calling himself God's servant and the son of God's handmaid, says he is weak, short-lived and little able to understand judgment and laws, and that even a perfect man counts for nothing without God's wisdom. He recalls that God chose him as king and judge of his people and commanded him to build a sanctuary and altar on the holy mountain, a copy of the holy tent. He asks God to send Wisdom, who sits by God's thrones, knew his works and was present at the world's making, so that she may guide him, make his works acceptable and make him worthy of his father's throne. He ends by observing that mortal thoughts are unstable, that the body weighs down the soul, and that people were taught what pleases God and were saved only through wisdom and God's holy spirit sent from on high.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 9
s: God is addressed as the God of the speaker's ancestors and Lord of mercy, who made all things by his word and formed man by his wisdom to have dominion over creatures. He chose the speaker as king and judge of his people, commanded the building of a sanctuary and altar on his holy mountain, and is asked to send Wisdom from his throne of glory. The prayer says no one gains knowledge of his counsel unless he gives wisdom and sends his holy spirit from on high.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 9
s: Wisdom is described as sitting by God on his thrones, being with him, knowing his works, and being present when he made the world. She understands what is pleasing in God's eyes and right according to his commandments. The speaker asks God to send her from the holy heavens so she can work with him, guide him prudently and guard him in her glory, and the prayer says people on earth were saved through wisdom.

l: speaker (the king, son of God's handmaid), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 9
s: The speaker prays as God's servant and the son of his handmaid, describing himself as weak, short-lived and with little power to understand judgment and laws. He says God chose him as king and judge of his people and commanded the building of a sanctuary and altar. He asks for Wisdom so that his works will be acceptable, he will judge righteously and he will be worthy of his father's throne.

l: man (humanity created by God), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 9
s: Humankind was formed by God's wisdom to have dominion over the creatures and to rule the world in holiness, righteousness and uprightness. The text says even a perfect man counts for nothing without God's wisdom, that mortal thoughts are unstable and plans prone to fail, and that a corruptible body weighs down the soul. People can hardly guess earthly things and cannot trace heavenly ones, but through wisdom their ways were corrected, they were taught what pleases God, and they were saved.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: Chapter 10 recounts how wisdom saved and guided a series of righteous figures from the first formed father of the world through the exodus. She guarded the first father and gave him strength to rule, while the unrighteous man who killed his brother perished in his own rage. She saved a righteous man from the flood by a piece of wood, preserved another blameless to God amid confounded nations, and delivered a righteous man from the fire that fell on the five cities, whose wickedness left a smoking waste and a pillar of salt. She guided a fugitive from his brother's wrath and prospered him, and she stayed with a sold righteous man in the dungeon until he received a kingdom's sceptre. Finally she delivered a holy people from a nation of oppressors through a servant of the Lord, led them over the Red sea, drowned their enemies, and moved them to praise God.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: Wisdom guards, delivers, guides and prospers the righteous throughout the chapter, from the first formed father to the holy people. She saves from the flood and the fire, stays with a righteous man in the dungeon, enters the soul of a servant of the Lord, brings the people over the Red sea, drowns their enemies, and opens the mouth of the mute and makes babes' tongues speak clearly.

l: one formed first (first-formed man), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: He was created alone and was guarded to the end by wisdom. She delivered him out of his own transgression and gave him strength to rule over all things.

l: unrighteous man (who killed his brother), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: He fell away from wisdom in his anger and killed his brother. He perished himself in the rage with which he did so.

l: righteous man (saved by wood in the flood), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: When the earth was drowning with a flood for the sake of the unrighteous man, wisdom saved it by guiding this righteous man's course by a paltry piece of wood.

l: righteous man (loved his child), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: When nations consenting together in wickedness were confounded, wisdom knew this righteous man and preserved him blameless to God. She kept him strong when his heart yearned toward his child.

l: righteous man (fled the fire on the five cities), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: Wisdom delivered him while the ungodly perished, as he fled from the fire that descended out of heaven on the five cities.

l: five cities, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: Fire descended out of heaven on them while the ungodly perished. A smoking waste, plants bearing fair fruit that doesn't ripen, and a standing pillar of salt remain as witnesses to their wickedness.

l: righteous man (fugitive from his brother's wrath), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: Wisdom guided him in straight paths while he fled his brother's wrath. She showed him God's kingdom, gave him knowledge of holy things, prospered his toils, stood by him against covetous men and enemies, and judged his severe conflict so that he would know godliness is more powerful than everyone.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: God is the one to whom wisdom preserved a righteous man blameless, and whose kingdom she showed to the fugitive righteous man. The righteous sang praise to his holy name and extolled his hand that fought for them.

l: righteous man (sold, imprisoned, then made ruler), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: He was sold, but wisdom did not forsake him and delivered him from sin. She went down with him into the dungeon and stayed with him in bonds until she brought him a kingdom's sceptre and authority over his tyrants, showed his mocking accusers to be false, and gave him eternal glory.

l: holy people, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: Wisdom delivered this holy people and blameless seed from a nation of oppressors. She rewarded their toils, guided them by a marvelous way, covered them by day and was a starry flame by night, and brought them over the Red sea. The righteous plundered the ungodly and sang praise to the Lord's holy name.

l: nation of oppressors, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: This nation oppressed the holy people and blameless seed, from whom wisdom delivered them. Its enemies were drowned and cast up from the bottom of the deep, and the righteous plundered the ungodly.

l: servant of the Lord, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: Wisdom entered into the soul of this servant of the Lord. He withstood terrible kings in wonders and signs.

l: Red sea, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 10
s: Wisdom brought the holy people over the Red sea and led them through much water. She drowned their enemies in it and cast them up from the bottom of the deep.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 11
s: Chapter 11 recounts how Wisdom prospered the works of the righteous under a holy prophet as they crossed a trackless desert, withstood foes, and received water from flinty rock when they thirsted and called on God. The same waters that benefited them became punishment for their enemies, whose river turned to clotted blood in rebuke of the decree to slay babies. God tested the righteous as a father admonishing, but searched out the ungodly as a stern king condemning, and the enemies came to recognize the Lord when they heard of the others' benefit. For their worship of irrational reptiles and vermin, God punished the ungodly with a multitude of irrational creatures, so they would learn that a man is punished by the very things through which he sins. The chapter closes by noting that God, though able to destroy by a single breath and arranging all things by measure, number, and weight, has mercy on all, loves all that exists, and spares all things because they are his.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 11
s: God gave the thirsting righteous water from the flinty rock and gave them abundant water beyond hope, while punishing their foes with blood in the river and with a multitude of irrational creatures. He tested the righteous as a father and condemned the ungodly as a stern king, is all-powerful and arranged all things by measure, number, and weight, and has mercy on all, loving all that he made and sparing all things because they are his.

l: Israelites (the righteous), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 11
s: The righteous traveled through a desert without inhabitants, pitched tents in trackless regions, and withstood enemies and repelled foes. When they thirsted they called on God and received water from the rock, and they learned through their trial, chastened in mercy, how the ungodly were tormented in wrath.

l: Egyptians (the ungodly enemies), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 11
s: The ungodly enemies saw their river turn to clotted blood as rebuke for the decree to slay babies, and they were distressed with double grief, groaning at the memory of past events. When they heard that the others benefited through their own punishments, they recognized the Lord, stopped mocking the one once thrown out and exposed, and marveled at a thirst unlike that of the righteous. Because they worshiped irrational reptiles and vermin, a multitude of irrational creatures was sent to punish them.

l: Wisdom, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 11
s: Wisdom is said to have prospered the works of the righteous in the hand of a holy prophet. This opens the chapter and frames the journey through the desert that follows.

l: water from the rock, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 11
s: Water was given from flinty, hard stone to the righteous when they thirsted and called on God, providing healing of their thirst. It was given abundantly and beyond hope, and it stood in contrast to the river turned to clotted blood, showing that the same things that punished foes benefited the righteous in need.

l: irrational creatures (reptiles and vermin), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 11
s: The ungodly were led astray to worship irrational reptiles and wretched vermin in their senseless imaginings. In return, God sent upon them a multitude of irrational creatures as punishment, though the text says he could equally have sent bears, lions, or newly created fire-breathing beasts.

l: divine mercy, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 11
s: God's mercy extends to all men because he has power to do all things, and he overlooks human sins so that they may repent. The text grounds this in his love for all that exists, his abhorrence of nothing he made, and his sparing of all things because they are his. The righteous were chastened in mercy, and the ungodly were not destroyed outright by a single breath.

l: sin and punishment, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 11
s: The chapter teaches that by what things a man sins, by these he is punished, as shown by the worship of reptiles being answered with creatures sent against the worshipers. Justice could have scattered the sinners by a breath, yet God arranged all things by measure, number, and weight, and punished the ungodly as a king while admonishing the righteous as a father.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 12
s: Chapter 12 addresses the Lord, whose incorruptible spirit is in all things and who corrects sinners gradually so they may repent. It describes the old inhabitants of the holy land, accused of enchantments, child slaughter and ritual banquets of flesh and blood, whom the Lord chose to destroy by the hands of 'our fathers' so the land could receive a worthy colony of God's servants. Instead of destroying them at once, the Lord sent hornets and judged them little by little, giving a chance to repent although he knew their wickedness was inborn. The text argues that the Lord's power is the source of his righteousness and that he judges in gentleness, which teaches his people to be kind and to hope for repentance and mercy. It ends with the unrighteous who lived in folly and worshipped despised animals as gods, who were mocked, then punished through those same creatures, and so came to recognize the true God.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 12
s: The Lord is addressed as having an incorruptible spirit in all things, who corrects sinners little by little and rules all things righteously. Though able to destroy the ungodly at once, he judges in gentleness and forbearance, no one can challenge his judgment, and his strength is the source of righteousness. He taught his people kindness and gives repentance to sinners, and he led the unrighteous to recognize him as the true God through their punishment.

l: old inhabitants of your holy land, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 12
s: They are described as practicing detestable enchantments and unholy rites, including merciless slaughter of children and sacrificial banquets of men's flesh and blood. The Lord's counsel was to destroy them by the hands of 'our fathers', yet he spared them as men, sent hornets ahead of the army, and judged them gradually to give them a chance to repent. The text says he knew their nature was evil and inborn and would not change, calling them a cursed seed from the beginning.

l: holy land, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 12
s: The holy land is called most precious of all in the Lord's sight. Its old inhabitants were destroyed so that it might receive a worthy colony of God's servants.

l: God's people (Israel, your sons), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 12
s: God's people, called 'your sons', are described as heirs of the Lord's oaths and covenants of good promises to their fathers, and their fathers were the instruments of destroying the land's old inhabitants. The Lord taught them through his dealings that the righteous must be kind, and gave them good hope because he gives repentance to sinners. When chastened, they are to ponder his goodness when they judge and look for mercy when they are judged, while their enemies are scourged ten thousand times more.

l: unrighteous who lived in folly, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 12
s: These people went far astray in error, taking as gods animals that even their enemies held in dishonor, and were deceived like foolish babes. The Lord first sent mocking judgment as to unreasoning children, then tormented them through their own abominations. Those who would not heed mild correction faced deserved judgment, and through being punished by the creatures they thought gods, they recognized the true God whom they had refused to know, after which extreme condemnation came upon them.

l: divine judgment, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 12
s: Divine judgment is portrayed as righteous, unchallengeable by any king, prince or avenger, and carried out gradually and with gentleness although the Lord has the power to act at once. It begins with mild correction and mockery and, for those who do not heed it, escalates to deserved punishment and extreme condemnation. It also serves as a model for God's people, who are to ponder his goodness when they judge.

l: repentance and forbearance, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 12
s: The Lord's forbearance is shown in judging offenders little by little, giving times and opportunities to escape wickedness, even to the old inhabitants of the land whose nature he knew would not change. It is rooted in his strength and sovereignty, and it teaches his people to be kind and gives them good hope because he gives repentance when men sin. Those who refuse mild correction eventually face the deserved judgment.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 13
s: Chapter 13 condemns men who lacked perception of God and failed to recognize the architect from his works, instead taking fire, wind, air, stars, water, or heavenly luminaries to be gods. It argues that if they admired the beauty or power of these things, they should understand that their Sovereign Lord, who created them, is far greater, and it grants these seekers small blame while still saying they are not excused for not finding him sooner. It then turns to those who call men's handiwork, such as gold, silver, animal likenesses, and stone, gods, and describes a woodcutter who saws down a tree, makes a useful vessel, cooks with the scraps, and carves a leftover knotty piece into the image of a man or animal. He paints it red, sets it in a wall secured with iron so it won't fall, and then prays to it for goods, marriage, children, health, life, aid, a safe journey, and success in business, though it is lifeless, weak, and unable to move or act.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 13
s: God is presented as the architect and first author of beauty who created the elements and heavenly bodies, and is far better and more powerful than they are. Mankind can form a corresponding perception of their Maker from the greatness of created things, and those who explored the world are faulted for not finding him sooner.

l: men who had no perception of God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 13
s: These men are called foolish by nature because they could not know him who exists from the good things seen and did not recognize the architect from his works. They thought fire, wind, air, stars, water, or luminaries were gods; those who sought God and were swayed by beauty receive small blame, but are still not excused, and those who worshiped handmade things are called miserable, with hopes in dead things.

l: nature worship (fire, wind, air, stars, water, luminaries), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 13
s: Fire, wind, swift air, circling stars, raging water, and luminaries of heaven were taken to be gods that rule the world. The text says that if people admired their beauty or power, they should instead recognize how much better and more powerful their Maker is.

l: idols (works of men's hands), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 13
s: Idols are described as gold and silver skillfully made, likenesses of animals, or a useless stone from an ancient hand. The carved wooden image is secured in a wall with iron because it cannot help itself, and it is lifeless, weak, without experience, unable to move a step, and has hands with no ability.

l: woodcutter, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 13
s: The woodcutter saws down a tree, strips its bark, and makes a useful vessel for his life's needs, then burns the scraps to cook and eat his fill. He takes a discarded, crooked, knotty piece, carves it in idleness into the image of a man or worthless animal, paints it red, sets it in a wall with iron, and prays to it without shame.

l: idolatry, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 13
s: Idolatry is depicted as praying to a lifeless object for goods, marriage, children, health, life, aid, a good journey, and success in business. The text shows its absurdity by noting that the one addressed is dead, weak, and unable to move, and must be secured by its maker so it won't fall.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 14
s: Chapter 14 begins with a seafarer who trusts a fragile piece of wood, and credits God's providence for giving a path through the sea, noting that wood saved the hope of the world on a raft when proud giants perished. It blesses the wood through which righteousness comes but curses the hand-made idol and its maker, since both are hateful to God and will be punished. The chapter traces the origin of idols to a grieving father's image of his dead child, to a custom hardened into law by princes, and to images of distant kings and an artisan's flattering beauty that drew the crowd to worship. It describes the resulting moral ruin, including child-slaughter, secret rites, adultery, murder, theft, perjury and disorder in marriage, calling idol worship the beginning, cause and end of every evil. It ends by declaring that worshipers who swear false oaths by lifeless idols will face the just penalty meant for sinners.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 14
s: God is addressed as Father whose providence guides ships, having given a way in the sea and a sure path in the waves, so that he can save from every danger. He guided the seed of mankind on a raft when proud giants perished, hates both the ungodly and his ungodliness, and will punish the deed together with the doer.

l: wood, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 14
s: Wood is shown as a fragile means by which sailors and rafts, under God's guidance, come safely to land, including the raft that carried the hope of the world. It is declared blessed when righteousness comes through it, in contrast with wood made into an idol, which is accursed.

l: idols (works of men's hands), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 14
s: Idols are described as hand-made things, formed from what God created, that were made an abomination, stumbling blocks to souls and a snare to the feet of the foolish. They did not exist from the beginning and will not last forever, because they entered the world through human boastfulness and a speedy end was planned for them. A visitation is coming upon them.

l: idolatry, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 14
s: Idolatry is traced to a grieving father's image of his dead child, then to a custom turned into law by the commands of princes, and to images of distant kings made to flatter them. An ambitious artisan's beautified likeness drew the crowd to devotion, and people in calamity or under tyranny gave stones and stocks the Name that shouldn't be shared. It is called the beginning of fornication, the corruption of life, and the beginning, cause and end of every evil.

l: worshipers, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 14
s: Worshipers of idols are said to go astray in the knowledge of God, live in a great war of ignorance, and call a multitude of evils peace. They make merry to madness, prophesy lies, live unrighteously and lightly swear false oaths, trusting lifeless idols to spare them from harm. Because they thought evil of God and despised holiness, the just doom will pursue them.

l: moral corruption, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 14
s: The chapter lists the consequences of idolatry as slaughtering children in rites, frenzied revels, treacherous killing, adultery, blood and murder, theft, deceit, faithlessness, tumult and perjury. It also names ingratitude, defiling of souls, confusion of sex and disorder in marriage, so that neither life nor purity of marriage is guarded.

l: divine judgment, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 14
s: Judgment is announced as punishment of the deed together with the one who committed it, and as a visitation among the idols of the nation. The chapter closes by saying that the just penalty for sinners, not the power of the things sworn by, always overtakes the transgression of the unrighteous, who swore falsely and thought evil of God.

l: The Wisdom of Solomon, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 15
s: The speaker addresses God as gracious, true, patient, and merciful, and says that the speakers, God's people, remain his even when they sin, since knowing him is perfect righteousness and the root of immortality. The chapter then ridicules idol makers, especially a potter who molds clay into vessels and also into a vain god, though he is himself made of earth and will soon return his borrowed soul. It says this potter is ignorant of the one who made him, treats life as a game for profit, and knows he sins. It also condemns the enemies of God's people who oppressed them and counted lifeless idols as gods, and it closes by saying that the creatures they worship are the most hateful and senseless, and lack God's praise and blessing.

l: God, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 15
s: God is addressed as gracious, true, patient, and in mercy ordering all things. Knowing him and his dominion is called perfect righteousness and the root of immortality, and he is the one who molded humans and breathed an active soul and vital spirit into them.

l: God's people (Israel, your sons), The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 15
s: The speakers say they are God's even if they sin, since they know his dominion, and that they will not sin, knowing they have been accounted his. They say they were not led astray by any evil human plan or by painters' labor on colored images. They were oppressed by enemies who worshiped idols.

l: potter, The Wisdom of Solomon, Chapter 15
s: The potter kneads soft earth and molds vessels for clean and contrary uses from the same clay, and he alone judges what each is for. He also labors to an evil end by molding a vain god from clay, though he was himself made of earth and must soon give back the soul lent to him. He is said to have a heart of ashes, to be ignorant of his Maker, to treat life as a game for profit, and to know he sins more than anyone else.
